title: Chess Terms for Beginners
description: Key chess rules, tactics, and vocabulary for new players, from castling and en passant to forks, pins, and the endgame.
subject: other

cards.definition: A single piece attacks two or more enemy pieces at the same time, so the opponent can't save them all.
The king moves two squares toward a rook, and that rook moves to the square the king passed over. Neither piece may have moved before, and the king may not castle out of, through, or into check.
When a pawn advances two squares and lands beside an enemy pawn, that pawn may capture it as if it had moved one square, but only on the next move.
The king is under direct attack. The player must get out of check on their next move.
The king is in check and has no legal way to escape. The game is over.
The player to move is not in check but has no legal moves. The game is a draw.
A piece can't move, or shouldn't, because doing so would expose a more valuable piece or the king behind it.
A valuable piece is attacked, and when it moves out of the way, a less valuable piece behind it can be captured.
Moving one piece out of the way reveals an attack by another piece behind it.
A pawn that reaches the far end of the board is replaced by a queen, rook, bishop, or knight of the same color.
A common rule of thumb: pawn 1, knight 3, bishop 3, rook 5, queen 9. The king can't be traded, so it has no point value.
The first phase of the game, focused on developing pieces, controlling the center, and getting the king to safety.
The phase after the opening, where most of the plans, attacks, and tactics play out.
The final phase, with few pieces left, where an active king and pushing pawns to promotion matter most.
Moving pieces off their starting squares to active positions, especially in the opening.
An opening that offers material, usually a pawn, in exchange for faster development or the initiative.
Deliberately giving up material to gain an advantage such as a strong attack or a better position.
A single move treated as a unit of time. Gaining a tempo means reaching a goal with one move fewer than expected.
A position where any move the player makes will worsen their position, but they are not allowed to pass.
Checkmate by a rook or queen along the king's home row, when the king is boxed in by its own pawns.
A player can claim a draw when the same position occurs three times with the same player to move.
A player can claim a draw after 50 moves by each side with no pawn move and no capture.
In formal games, if you deliberately touch one of your pieces, you must move it if it has a legal move.
The standard way to record moves, naming squares by file (a to h) and rank (1 to 8), as in Nf3.
